nature-econ-864.title: Black markets: trade the law forbids
nature-econ-864.text:
Illegal logging is, according to Interpol, an industry worth almost as much as drug production in some countries. It is one face of the black market: a clandestine market, or set of transactions, with some aspect of illegality within a legal jurisdiction. It is a {{ref:nature-econ-342}} that operates out of sight.

Transactions in goods whose production or distribution the law prohibits or restricts are black-market trade because the exchange itself is illegal. Such goods may be cheaper than legal ones because suppliers avoid production costs and taxes. In many developing countries wild animals are captured and sold as pets, or hunted for meat, hides and organs used in traditional medicine.

nature-econ-863.title: Barriers to entry: what keeps newcomers out
nature-econ-863.text:
A new firm often faces a cost that the firms already in the market never had to pay. That is a barrier to entry: a fixed cost a new entrant must bear to enter a market that incumbents do not bear or have not had to bear.

By protecting incumbents and restricting competition, barriers can distort prices, which is why they matter most in antitrust policy. They often cause or help sustain a {{ref:nature-econ-349}} or oligopoly, or give firms market power. Governments can also erect them, for instance to meet consumer protection laws.

A primary barrier is a cost that is a barrier on its own. An ancillary barrier only reinforces other barriers that are present. A structural barrier comes from inherent industry conditions such as upfront capital, economies of scale and network effects. A strategic barrier is created or raised by existing firms, for example by exclusive contracts.

The height of barriers separates market types. {{ref:nature-econ-353}} has zero barriers to entry, monopolistic competition allows medium barriers, and oligopoly typically has high ones. Porter classes markets by entry and exit barriers: the higher both are, the more prone a market is to natural monopoly, and the lower, the nearer to perfect competition.

Economists have offered conflicting definitions since the 1950s. Bain (1956), Stigler (1968), Fisher (1979), Baumol and Willig (1981) and others each gave one, and no consensus exists on which to use.

nature-econ-865.title: Public utilities: essential services under public control
nature-econ-865.text:
A public utility is an organization that maintains the infrastructure for a public service, often also providing the service itself. Utilities supply goods considered essential, such as water, gas, electricity, telephone and waste disposal, and are subject to public control or regulation.

The reason is the cost structure. Utilities are capital-intensive, with large economies of scale and high fixed costs for plants, lines and treatment facilities. Electricity transmission lines and natural gas pipelines have the traits of a {{ref:nature-econ-350}}: where infrastructure exists, competing brings little benefit. In the US, public utilities commissions regulate electric, gas, telecom, water and rail companies, approving or denying rate increases on behalf of ratepayers.

In 1996, FERC Order No. 888 required electric utilities to open their transmission systems and unbundle transmission from other operations. That restructured the regulated {{ref:nature-econ-349}} toward competition among bulk sellers.

Modern utilities may draw partly or wholly on clean and renewable energy, mostly wind turbines and solar panels. In OECD countries, wholesale electricity generation has become far more decentralised with solar and wind power, while distribution and transmission networks often stay centralised and need heavy government involvement.

nature-econ-866.title: Utility rate regulation: three ways to cap a price
nature-econ-866.text:
Regulators of a {{ref:nature-econ-865}} have three common tools for setting the price it may charge. Average-cost pricing sets the price equal to average production cost at the break-even point, serving most of the market, but regulated firms then lack incentive to minimise costs.

Rate-of-return regulation lets firms set any price so long as the return on invested capital stays under a cap. It is flexible but can cause overcapitalization, since investing more capital raises the allowed profit. Price cap regulation directly sets a maximum price, which can result in a loss of service area.

nature-econ-859.title: Product differentiation: making one product stand apart
nature-econ-859.text:
Edward Chamberlin proposed the concept in his 1933 book on monopolistic competition. Product differentiation is the process of distinguishing a product from competitors' and from a firm's other products to make it more attractive to a target market. It is inconsistent with perfect competition, which needs identical products.

Vertical differentiation rests on a characteristic consumers can rank objectively, such as quality. Horizontal differentiation rests on subjective taste, such as colour. Mixed differentiation combines both. Sources include quality, functional features or design, buyers' ignorance, advertising and availability in time and place. Buyers must perceive the difference. A green product may have lower environmental harm yet be inferior in other respects, so its appeal depends on advertising and social pressure.

The pricing effect is direct. A firm cannot charge a higher price if products are good substitutes, and the further a product departs from others in its segment, the higher the price it can charge. Low differentiation makes collusion harder to hold, since a small price cut can win a large share of the market.

nature-econ-857.title: Collusion: when rivals quietly stop competing
nature-econ-857.text:
In 2019 the European Commission found that BMW, Daimler and Volkswagen had colluded to hold back improvements in vehicle emissions technology. Collusion is an agreement or secret cooperation among firms or individuals to limit competition, for example by dividing a market, fixing prices or limiting output.

It often arises in an {{ref:nature-econ-364}}. Price fixing harms consumers, so it is illegal under antitrust law and participants keep it secret. Tacit collusion is considered legal.

A collusive price is unsustainable in a one-off game because members have an incentive to deviate. It needs repeated interaction and firms that value future profits. With n symmetric firms, the cartel is stable only if the discount factor is at least (n-1)/n, so more firms make collusion harder to sustain. Other barriers include cost and demand differences and asymmetric information. High concentration, homogeneous products and stable demand or excess capacity favour it.

Governments respond with fines and imprisonment, screening markets for suspicious pricing, and leniency for the first firm to confess.

nature-econ-862.title: Vertical integration: owning the supply chain
nature-econ-862.text:
In the US, 90% of poultry, 69% of hogs and 29% of cattle are produced under contracts that act as vertical integration. It is an arrangement in which a company owns and controls several stages of its supply chain. It contrasts with horizontal integration, where a company produces several related items, and comes as backward (upstream), forward (downstream) or balanced.

A firm integrates to secure the supplies it needs and the market for its product. The real net output ratio, added value over total production value, measures it: the less a firm outsources, the closer the ratio is to one. Gains include synchronising supply and demand, capturing upstream or downstream margins and lower uncertainty. Losses include higher switching costs, weaker performance incentives upstream and specific investments.

For society, it can lower consumer prices by cutting intermediary markups, but it can enable price manipulation where market power is established, and it becomes undesirable when it turns anti-competitive.

Electricity shows both sides. Before late-20th-century deregulation, most US electric utilities were vertically integrated across generation, transmission, distribution and sales. PURPA in 1978 forced them to buy outside power if competitive, giving rise to independent producers.

nature-econ-858.title: Bertrand competition: rivals undercutting down to cost
nature-econ-858.text:
If two firms sell the same good and compete on price, what happens? Bertrand proposed in 1883, as a reply to Cournot, that firms should undercut rivals' prices whenever those exceed marginal cost. Edgeworth formalised the idea in 1889. The model of oligopoly it produced has firms selling identical goods compete by setting prices, while buyers choose the quantities. It is the price-setting counterpart of {{ref:nature-econ-302}}.

It assumes identical goods, equal marginal costs, no capacity limits, simultaneous price setting and no search costs, so the lowest-priced firm takes the whole market. The only equilibrium is price equal to marginal cost, with zero profit. It is a weak Nash equilibrium because deviating costs nothing.

Relax the assumptions and the result shifts. Product differentiation, transport or search costs remove the result that price falls to marginal cost. With capacity constraints (the Bertrand-Edgeworth model) a pure-strategy equilibrium may not exist, the Edgeworth paradox. With network effects, firms may price aggressively to enlarge their customer base.

Bertrand industries are more competitive than Cournot ones because prices are strategic complements while quantities are strategic substitutes. Bertrand suits flexible capacity, and Cournot suits output set in advance.

nature-econ-856.title: Diffusion of innovations: how new ideas spread
nature-econ-856.text:
Why do some new technologies sweep through a society while others stall? Diffusion of innovations is a theory of how, why and how fast new ideas and technologies spread through a social system. Everett Rogers popularised it in 1962, describing diffusion as an innovation being communicated through channels over time among members of a social system. It is a close companion to {{ref:nature-econ-318}}.

Study of diffusion took off in 1920s and 1930s rural sociology, which examined how independent US farmers adopted hybrid seeds, equipment and techniques. The unit of adoption is usually an individual but can be an organization, a network cluster or a country. Diffusion follows a five-step decision process.

Rate of adoption is the time a share of a social system takes to adopt. Rogers sorted adopters into five categories by innovativeness, and uptake follows an S curve over time. The model predicts growth to a saturation level then decline, but cannot say how long it takes or what the saturation level will be.

Diffusion can fail to approach full adoption because of weaknesses, rival innovations or lack of awareness, or be widely taken up in some clusters but not others. Adoption can have public consequences for others and private ones for the adopter, benefits and costs, and unintended negative effects.

nature-econ-860.title: Marginal revenue productivity: what a worker adds is what a worker earns
nature-econ-860.text:
In this neoclassical model, wages equal the marginal revenue product of labour, the extra revenue an added unit of labour brings. A profit-maximising firm hires workers until marginal revenue product equals the wage, since a worker whose marginal revenue is below the wage would cut profit.

Marginal revenue product is marginal product times marginal revenue, so hiring stops where MR times MP equals the wage, equivalent to MR equals MC. In perfect competition MRP equals marginal physical product times price. A monopoly or imperfect competitor faces falling prices, so its MRP curve slopes down faster.

nature-econ-861.title: Stackelberg competition: the advantage of moving first
nature-econ-861.text:
Heinrich von Stackelberg described this sequential game in 1934. A leader firm chooses its quantity first, and follower firms then respond, competing on quantity. It needs a leader with commitment power, and the follower must observe the leader's move and be unable to commit to other actions.

It is solved by backward induction: the leader anticipates the follower's best response and picks the quantity maximising its own payoff. Moving first gives the leader an advantage over {{ref:nature-econ-302}}. If the follower cannot observe the leader's move, the game reduces to that Cournot case.

Outcomes sit between the extremes. Stackelberg output exceeds Cournot output but is below Bertrand output, and its price is lower than Cournot's but higher than Bertrand's. Its price also lies below the monopoly or cartel price but above the perfectly competitive price.

nature-econ-850.title: Income distribution: who gets the national income
nature-econ-850.text:
Income distribution describes how a country's total income, or GDP, is shared among its population. Classical economists such as Smith, Malthus and Ricardo studied factor income distribution, while modern economists focus on distribution across individuals and households. In neoclassical theory, national income is distributed according to factor prices, the payment to each factor of production.

Inequality is distinct from poverty and fairness. The Gini coefficient measures it from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality), and the Lorenz curve can depict it. Policies that shape it include progressive taxation and public spending on education, healthcare and social security for lower-income groups.

The Kuznets curve holds that inequality rises as a country develops and falls once average income reaches a certain level, though many prominent economists disagree that rising inequality is necessary. Income mobility, how people move in the earnings hierarchy over their lifetime, is measured by the association between parents' and adult children's socioeconomic standing.

Institutions matter too. Unionization reduces wage inequality: for American male workers the reduction was 1.7 percent in the private sector and 16.2 percent in the public sector.
